account:
It is eight o'clock on day 1, and I am at the town hall with the secretary and freight, ready for office hours. I read today's appointment book and have just returned it to the secretary: mill grain inspection at ten, lunch at home, council letters at one, tea with the neighbour at the dockside cottage at three, office at four-thirty, and home at seven.

The notable issue is the lack of written business records so far. Yesterday the great hall table chests were empty, and the treasury held emeralds but I found no accounts. The secretary says there are no overnight letters or written inspection reports, though yesterday's office record is now in the appointments chest. I do not know why there are no accounts; this alone does not establish wrongdoing.

The builder reported no confirmed damage along the bridge and east-bank routes, lanterns present, and no expenditure. His west-bank inspection remains outstanding. He wants an identified repair scope and payment terms; I have not approved repair spending without identified work and an itemized estimate. My evening reply to him was not heard, so I should not assume he received those further instructions.

Freight has come to ask about scheduled deliveries or transport work. He says his warehouse is empty, the ferry is at the east landing, and he has no new quay news. This appears to be an effort to arrange work in advance, not evidence of an unusual shipment. I told him I know of no town transport orders and will ask about transport needs at the mill inspection. The secretary is remaining here to receive visitors and correspondence. For now, town business seems quiet, with inspection and transport proposals awaiting concrete needs rather than approved purchases.
